items.article: Hero passenger Yaniv claims he helped control FlyDubai flight FZ1073 using skills he picked up from a TV show after one of the pilots allegedly tried to crash it yesterday A hero passenger who "broke into the cockpit" of FlyDubai flight FZ1073 before controlling the plane, following an alleged attempted by one pilot to crash it yesterday, said he learnt how to land the jet after watching a TV show. FlyDubai flight FZ1073 issued an emergency hijacking alert yesterday morning while en route to Tel Aviv after one of the pilots allegedly stabbed another and tried to crash the aircraft. The injured pilot and passengers bravely fought back control of the plane, which eventually landed in Saudi Arabia. Yaniv, who Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu described as a "great hero", was one of the passengers who helped. He explained: "I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and pulled him - first and foremost - outside." He said he then pulled at the controls. Yaniv claimed knew how to control the plane after watching a TV show on major aviation disasters, Air Crash Investigation. Mr Netanyahu alleged one of the pilots " stabbed the other pilot and apparently tried to crash the plane". The wounded pilot who has been named as Indian national Smit Machchhar, is said to have opened the cockpit door so passengers and crew could stop the attacker. items.article: Bel Mooney dives into the world of sculpture and discovers how often artists have tried to capture our humanity through the natural objects around us. Published: 17:00, 29 August 2026 | Updated: 17:00, 29 August 2026 Pick up a pebble, large or small. Cradle it and weigh its smooth plainness, or notice its bands of colour. You probably don’t think of it as a mini work of art, and yet renowned 20th-century sculptors such as Barbara Hepworth and Henry Moore would have done. They found inspiration in the forms of the natural world – works of ‘art’ created by time. Standing on a beach, art historian Jo Baring thinks of the delight children have always found in pebbles. Right at the beginning of this beautifully written book, she identifies the magic at its heart: ‘The pebble… acts as a physical reminder of our connection to both material [substance] and what we make… For millennia, our ancestors have moulded, modelled and chiselled the materials they had to hand, creating objects with no immediate practical use.’ Art: Antony Gormley's Angel of the North is ‘a totem pole for the North East’ So, not pots or combs or arrowheads, but things created – from stone or wood or metal – to convey a feeling or message. In other words, they have created sculpture. You may think of this art form in terms of the powerfully expressive bronze statue of Sir Winston Churchill in Parliament Square, London, created by the Welsh sculptor Ivor Roberts-Jones.
